tier_reason: Public harness (src/gpu/bench_gpu.cu, src/gpu/spmv_cusparse.cu, scripts/run_gpu.sh) with committed results (results/gpu/timings.csv), compiler and flags in src/Makefile (nvcc 12.3, -O3 -arch=sm_80 -std=c++14 -Xcompiler -O3) and the GPU named (A100 80GB), so it meets A as a reproducible first-party run against cuSPARSE; the README table numbers match the CSV.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: src/Makefile: nvcc (CUDA 12.3 per README) -O3 -arch=sm_80 -lineinfo -std=c++14 --ptxas-options=-v -Xcompiler -O3, linked with -lcusparse -lcublas; CPU build gcc -O3 -march=native -ftree-vectorize.
corrections.caveats: Coursework-style project with four real matrices, one A100 run, 1 warm-up plus 10 timed single-call iterations. Bandwidth figures use a formula that counts every x[col] read as DRAM traffic, which is why they exceed the 1555 GB/s peak (98-110 percent); the CSR arrays themselves are about 48-72 MB (derived from page data), so this is x-vector reuse in L2, not the whole matrix fitting in cache. Only cuSPARSE CSR_ALG2 was compared, and each timed cuSPARSE call uses a freshly created handle and descriptors with no reuse or preprocessing. In results/gpu/timings.csv cuSPARSE takes about 0.021-0.025 ms on the 10K-row synthetic matrices where the custom kernels take about 0.007-0.010 ms, and the absolute gaps on cant, consph and pdb1HYS are 0.016, 0.019 and 0.028 ms (derived from page data), so much of the 24-56 percent win may be cuSPARSE per-call overhead rather than kernel efficiency. cuSPARSE is 4.2x faster on webbase-1M. No LICENSE file, so reference only.

notes: README table matches results/gpu/timings.csv exactly (e.g. cant 0.052838 ms vector vs 0.069018 ms cuSPARSE). Tier A holds on the reproducibility rule, but the cuSPARSE timing setup is a fairness shortcoming worth recording. Metadata: no license file (LICENSE 404, none shown on github.com), 0 stars, 4 commits all on 2026-05-08 (active).

tier_reason: plots/scaling.csv (AMD EPYC 7763) is reproduced by public scripts (scripts/build.sh, scripts/scaling.sh, bin/main.cpp) that build SuiteSparse AMD v7.10.1 and ParAMD, with GCC 13.2.1 stated in the README and a Release build forced by CMakeLists.txt; code, compiler, flags and CPU are all public, so A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC v13.2.1 with OpenMP; CMakeLists.txt defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release; scripts/build.sh builds SuiteSparse v7.10.1 (AMD only) with its CMake defaults; scripts/scaling.sh runs seeds 1-5 with OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 or 64 and OMP_PLACES=cores.
corrections.caveats: Authors' own benchmark (PASSIONLab, arXiv preprint 2504.17097, whose abstract reports up to 8.30x; the paper itself could not be opened here and no peer-reviewed venue was confirmed). The committed plots/scaling.csv is one exemplar run on one machine. The headline speedups compare 64 threads to the single-threaded SuiteSparse AMD, so they measure parallel scaling, not per-core efficiency; at 1 thread ParAMD is slower on 8 of 9 matrices. Ordering quality drops slightly (fill-in up to 1.16x SuiteSparse's on nlpkkt240). Repository is young (4 commits, April to November 2025) and has few users.

notes: All nine speedups, single-thread ratios and fill-in ratios in the record match plots/scaling.csv. The record's 'SuiteSparse AMD version not stated' was wrong: build.sh pins SuiteSparse v7.10.1. tier_reason: First-party Google Benchmark run (benchmark/fmm_bench via run_benchmarks.sh, Release build) on an 8-core Apple M1 Pro laptop, with raw output committed in benchmark_plots/benchmark_output_example/; the compiler is not stated, so it falls short of A and stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'Reach >1GB/s read and write speeds on a laptop (about 25x improvement over IOStreams).' Committed example output (benchmark_plots/benchmark_output_example/cpp-8-Core Apple M1 Pro Laptop.json, 2023-05-27): coordinate read 1578 MB/s at 8 threads (peak 1598 MB/s at 6) vs sequential IOStream 48.5 MB/s, about 32.5x; 1 thread 500 MB/s, about 10.3x. Coordinate write 691 MB/s at 8 threads vs IOStream 60.9 MB/s, about 11.3x; 1 thread 217 MB/s, about 3.6x. Array read 1477 MB/s and array write 1020 MB/s at 8 threads (ratios derived from page data). Python bindings read coordinate files at 1652 MB/s vs the old SciPy mmread at 51.0 MB/s.
corrections.hardware: 8-core Apple M1 Pro laptop (README plot titles and committed benchmark JSON)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: run_benchmarks.sh: CMake -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; compiler not stated
corrections.caveats: This is sparse matrix file I/O, not a solver or kernel, so it is at the edge of the category. The IOStreams baseline is sequential by the author's choice (IOStreams slow down with threads because of locale locking), so most of the headline ratio is parallelism; single-thread gains are about 10x for reads and 3.6x for writes (derived from page data). '>1GB/s write' holds for array files only; coordinate writes peak at 691 MB/s. Compiler and C++ standard library are not stated; the README's detailed comparison sits in the separate parse-bench repo, which was not opened.

notes: README claim quoted correctly; numbers behind the README plots are in the committed example JSON, so claimed_speedup now carries them. Metadata: BSD-2-Clause (LICENSE.txt), 91 stars, 290 commits, not archived or a fork, last commit 2024-06-03 (stale).
